Today, I came across Aurora and then I understand that why AWS created a whole separate database
for relational databases instead of RDS.
So Aurora is proprietary Amazon database for relational databases such as MySQL and Postgres.
So why is it better than RDS and why should you use Aurora over RDS is that it is cloud
optimized.
It claims that they can provide 5x better performance on MySQL queries and 3x better performance
on Postgres queries.
Along with it, it provides automatic scaling options and it can manage up to 15 read replicas
by itself.
High availability is its native so you don't have to worry about that.
But the only thing is that it is 20% more expensive than an RDS service.
How it is compensated is that by paying more money you get high performance and it is more
effective than an RDS service.

So, today I explored disaster recovery, it is similar like read replicas but in this
we just use the database as a backup so that if any disaster happens in any data center
of AWS you would have your data backed up in another availability zone.
So read replicas are used for reading the data from the database so that your main
database is not overloaded and in disaster recovery what we do is we make another database
and place it in another availability zone so that if any mishap occurs in one availability
zone or in one data center of AWS your data is still backed up in another availability
zone.
So it is primarily for recovery and saving the data from mishaps.
So this was all about read replicas and disaster recovery in RDS service.
So these features are provided to you by default in an RDS service and if you setup

how a DNS system works. For example, you type in instagram.com in your web browser and Instagram
appears. How did this all happen? So whenever you type in a domain in your web browser, what happens is
that this domain is converted into an IP address of the server of Instagram. The very first step
in this is your browser sends this request to your local DNS server, which is mostly managed
by your computer or your ISP provider. If that domain is registered in your local DNS,
then your web browser sends that request to the IP address which was returned by your local DNS.
For example, your local DNS server do not know the IP address of Instagram.com. In that case,
the request is sent to root level DNS server, which is managed by ICANN and just in case,
if that root level domain name server do not know the IP address of your Instagram.com,
in that case, the request is sent to top level domain DNS server. And in case, TLD DNS server
is also not aware of your IP address of the Instagram.com. In that case, the request is
sent to secondary level DNS server, which are your domain providers just like GoDaddy,
Hostingers or Namecheap. So they will return an IP address, which will be returned to your
local DNS and it will be stored in a cache so that whenever you visit Instagram.com
next time your local DNS server is aware of the IP address of that requested website.
So this is how the DNS works under the hood.

Most people do not realize this that DNS is what make your website reachable to the internet.
DNS stands for domain name system. It is actually the backbone of the whole internet system.
Whenever we type in a domain, let's say www.google.com, what happens is that this domain
is converted into an IP address like 198.168.10 or something like that.

server where the request of this domain is going to be sent. And the only objective of using domain
name system is to make human friendly IP addresses. You can access a website with an IP address as well
but that would be too much tricky for humans to memorize the IP addresses of day to day website.

Today I explored what are Record Types and Hosted Zones for Route 53.
There are total 4 type record types in which we have A-Type C-Name and Name Servers.
The A-Type records maps the hostname with an IPv4 address and AAAA type of records maps
the hostname with an IPv6 IP address.
C-Name maps a hostname with an other hostname and Name Servers controls how traffic is
routed to a domain.
Now coming toward what are Hosted Zones.
Hosted Zones are basically containers that control how a traffic is routed to a domain
and there are 2 types of Hosted Zones.
Public Hosted Zones and Private Hosted Zones.
What Public Hosted Zones do is that it contains the record that specifies how the traffic
is routed to a domain.
So it is used to access the publicly available IP address.
On the other hand, the Private Hosted Zones contains the records that specify
how to route traffic from one VPC to another.

Most people think one EC2 instance can only be attached with one storage device, but that's totally wrong.
If we want that one server should be connected to at least more than one server at a time,
so in that case we can use EFS, which is Elastic File System.
It is just like a network storage device which is connected to our EC2 instance by network ports
and the best advantage of using EFS is that one EFS volume can be connected to at least 16 instances at a time.
And above that what it provides is that unlike EBS volumes that were availability zone bound, EFS is not bound by availability zones.
So which means that you can attach an EBEFS volume to an instance that is not available in your current availability zone in which your instance is available.
For example, if your instance is in US East 1 and your EFS volume is US East 2, you can connect both of these services.
And if you want to connect another instance with that EFS volume that is in US East 2, you can do that as well.
And you can connect up to 16 instances to that one single EFS volume.
But the only caveat here is it is super expensive and it is three times more expensive than a normal EBS volume.
So that was all about EFS and I am making comprehensive notes of AWS.

Most people do not realize this that every storage on EC2 is not permanent.
Today is the 11th of learning AWS and I explore what are EC2 instance stores.
EC2 instance stores are basically a physical hard drive that is mounted on your EC2 instance.
So it is just like a local storage device of your EC2 instance.
Unlike your EBS volumes which were connected to your EC2 instance via network ports.
So they are not connected via network. That means their latency would be super fast.
But here's the caveat. If your instance is stopped or terminated that would result in losing your data.
So EC2 instance store can be used for temporary storages like buffering,
caching, file uploading and etc. But it cannot be utilized as a permanent storage device for
your instance. So that was all about EC2 instance store and in the next videos I will

In order to save your cost in cloud computing, while scaling a system, all you need to know
is the two different types of scalability. One is vertical scalability and the other is horizontal
scalability. I will tell you the major differences between both of them. In vertical scaling,
what we do is try to upgrade the compute power, the RAM of our instance. For example,
upgrading an EC2 instance from T2 micro to T3 micro or another upgraded variant of the instance.
So in this, we basically try to add more RAM, more CPU, more hard drive so that our single instance
is capable of handling a lot of load per second. While in horizontal scaling, we try to add a lot
of instances of similar application so that the load or the incoming request can be distributed
across the multiple instances. So this is the major difference between two types of scaling.

and by now it will be depreciated.
The number 2 instance is ALB that stands for Application load balancer
and it is mostly used for web apps and it works on layer 7.
So it has options to divide the traffic on the basis of hostname,
query parameters and on the basis of routes as well.
For example, you have 2 instances and you want that
slash login should be directed to instance 1 and slash users should be directed to your instance 2.
In this case, you should use the application load balancer.
Then comes NLB network load balancer which is super fast and has ultra low latency
because it works on layer 3 of network layers.
Then we have Gateway load balancer which is a bit advanced

Today I learned what are routing policies in Route 53.
So the first type of routing policy I learned was latency based routing policy in which the user is
redirected to the resource that is nearest to him. For example, a user is requesting for a resource
from Pakistan. So according to the AWS Resources Regions, according to AWS Regions, the nearest
region to Pakistan is Mumbai. So most probably that user will be redirected to Mumbai region.
So this is called the latency based routing policy. Now coming towards the second routing
policy, which is failover routing policy in which we have to enable the health checks of
the resources so that we might be aware of which resources or instances are healthy,
so that the traffic could be redirected to the healthy resources for instance.
Next we have geo location routing policy in which the routing is based upon the client's
new location that his country, his continent. So if there is some AWS region in his own
country, he would be redirected towards that AWS region or if there is any AWS region
in his continent, then he will be, if there is no AWS region in his country, then he will be
redirected to the resource for instance that is available in his continent.
So this is all about the routing policy, routing policy and I am making comprehensive

Csit and Cse, which one is the best.
So, Csit, we keep Cse computer system engineering in one place and compare it separately.
So, Cse means that you want to become a programmer, you want to build software and you have more interest in software.
Cse on the other hand is more particularly hardware related degree.
And these two are totally different, although in this, you may be taught a little bit of software programming,
but when it comes to computer science, then with your hardware, there will be no communication at all.
You don't have to deal with the hardware, you don't have to build systems hardware wise.
Your work will be particularly software related.
So, first of all, these two differences have been cleared for you.
So, if your hardware related concepts are more interested in hardware, then you have come to know that Cse is the thing for you.
But if you think that my interest in software is more, then computer science is the thing.
But now coming towards Cse and IT, then computer science, software engineering, IT,
these three or four degrees that are exactly the same.
Their 70% subjects are exactly the same.
In the fifth or sixth semester, you will be given only a few electives on the basis of which your degree differentiates from Cse in IT and software engineering.
Other initial subjects are exactly the same.
So, you can just pick one and in that, I would suggest that you should go into computer science
because computer science is a much broader field than IT, software engineering, AI, TETA science or whatever the domains that are available.
So, in this, it is broader that you have more options for electives.
So, I would say that if you want to do Cse, then just go for Cse.
And if you are interested in hardware related things, then you can go for computer system engineering.

text:
Hey, no need to panic or think about dropping out — that's not the right move. AI isn't replacing software engineers; it's changing how we work, not eliminating the field. A few facts worth keeping in mind:
- AI tools can generate code, but they can't fully understand real-world problems, design system architecture, or make judgment calls about tradeoffs. That's still on the engineer.
- Every major tech shift (calculators, the internet, IDE autocomplete) triggered the same "this job is dead" fear. Each time, the field adapted and grew instead of disappearing.
- Companies increasingly need people who can review, debug, and validate AI-generated code — that requires solid fundamentals, not less of them.
What actually matters during your degree:
1. **Master the fundamentals** — data structures, algorithms, OOP concepts, how systems actually work under the hood. This is what AI can't replace, because it requires genuine understanding.
2. **Build real projects**, even small ones. Applying concepts yourself builds problem-solving skills no AI shortcut can substitute.
3. **Learn to read and debug code**, not just write it. Being able to spot what's wrong (including in AI-generated code) is a skill that's becoming more valuable, not less.
4. **Use AI as a tool, not a crutch.** Let it help you learn faster, but don't let it think for you — the goal is to understand *why* something works, not just get output.
5. **Stay adaptable.** The tools will keep changing; the ability to learn and problem-solve is what carries you through any shift.
Dropping out over this would be throwing away your future over fear, not facts. Stay in, focus on understanding — not memorizing — and you'll be fine.

🎓 𝗔𝗹𝗵𝗮𝗺𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗵! 𝗕𝗦𝗖𝗦 Completed (2022–2026) 🎓 

Today, I close one of the most memorable chapters of my life as I complete my Bachelor of Science in Computer Science from The Islamia University of Bahawalpur.

When I look back at these 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀, the first thing that comes to mind isn't the exams, grades, or assignments; it's the people and the memories. The countless hours spent with friends in classrooms, cafeterias, university grounds, and during group projects. The laughter before presentations, the stress before deadlines, the last-minute assignment submissions, the discussions about the future, and all those moments that seemed ordinary at the time but have now become some of my favorite memories.

University 𝘁𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 me much more than technical skills. It taught me how to manage responsibilities, work under pressure, meet deadlines, collaborate with others, and keep moving forward even when things became difficult. Balancing studies alongside professional work and client projects wasn't always easy, but it helped me grow both personally and professionally.

Throughout this 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆, I continued building websites, working with clients, learning new technologies, and gaining real-world experience. Every challenge became a lesson, and every project became an opportunity to improve.

Most importantly, I'm grateful for the 𝗳𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀, 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 that made these years special. While our classes may be over, the memories created during this journey will stay with us for a lifetime.

For my Final Year Project, I built a Smart University Bus Information System that digitizes a paper-based transport schedule into a live web platform. The system features a full-stack distributed architecture with two microservices , one built on NestJS/PostgreSQL for real-time bus tracking and another on Node.js/MongoDB for timetable management paired with a React frontend. Key features include real-time bus tracking, a custom crowd estimation algorithm, automated student alerts, and ETA calculations, with Redis caching for optimized performance. The entire system is containerized with Docker, deployed across hybrid cloud infrastructure (AWS EC2 and Vercel), and backed by a CI/CD pipeline via GitHub Actions.

A huge thank you to my teachers, classmates, friends, and family who were part of this journey. Here's to new beginnings, bigger goals, and the next chapter ahead. 

 Stay 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 for upcoming project updates and a detailed look into exciting work I've been building recently.

#csgrads

When I first heard about Redis, I thought it was something only "big companies" needed.

I was wrong.

I added Redis to my FYP to solve two very real, very student-sized problems:

Problem 1 → My OTP flow was querying the database on every verification attempt. Redis replaced that with a 5-minute in-memory store that auto-expires. Clean. Fast. Simple.

Problem 2 → My timetable page made the same DB call over and over. The data hadn't changed. Yet the query kept running. Redis cached it. Problem gone.

What I didn't expect:

→ How easy it was to get started (seriously, 30 minutes to set up)

→ How much it changed the way I think about data  "does this need to live in the DB, or just in memory for now?

→ That caching isn't just about speed  it's about reducing load, cost, and failure points

Redis taught me something beyond the tool itself:

Not every problem needs a database. Sometimes fast memory is the right answer.

What tools did you learn during your Final Year Project that changed how you think?

#Redis #FinalYearProject #StudentDeveloper #BackendDevelopment #Caching #LessonsLearned #TechCareers

Caching is not an optimization. It's a necessity , and Redis made me understand why.

During my FYP, I implemented Redis for two specific use cases:

𝟏. OTP Storage

Instead of writing OTPs to the database and querying them on verification, I pushed them to Redis with a TTL of 5 minutes.

Why this matters:

=> OTPs are temporary by nature. A DB record doesn't expire on its own.

=> Redis TTL handles expiry automatically. No cron job. No manual delete.

=> Verification became a single in-memory lookup instead of a DB round-trip.

𝟐. Timetable Caching

Timetables don't change every minute. But my app was querying the DB like they did.

Redis let me:

=> Cache the timetable data after the first fetch

=> Serve all subsequent requests from memory

=> Set cache invalidation when an update actually happens

The read pressure on my database dropped significantly.

Tools used: Node.js + ioredis client + Redis on the backend

If you're a student building your FYP  don't overlook caching. Your DB will thank you.

#Redis #Caching #BackendDevelopment #NodeJS #FinalYearProject #SoftwareEngineering #SystemDesign

In my Final Year Project (Digitized the University Bus timetable schedule with Real-Time Tracking of Buses ), I had two major bottlenecks:

→ OTP requests hitting the database every few seconds

→ Timetable data being fetched repeatedly on every page load.

Both of these were unnecessary reads. The data didn't change that often  yet every user request was going straight to the DB, creating a READ Pressue on the DB.

That's when I discovered Redis.

Redis is an in-memory data store , blazing fast, dead simple to use, and perfect for caching data that you read often but update rarely.

Here's what I did:

→ Stored OTPs in Redis with a TTL (time-to-live) of 5 minutes , auto-expiry, no manual cleanup needed.

→ Cached timetable data in Redis , served from memory instead of reading directly from the DB.

The result? My database pressure reduced alot. Response times dropped. And my app felt snappier.

If you're building anything with repeated reads , user sessions, configs, OTPs, frequently accessed data , give Redis a try.

It's one of those tools that makes you feel smart the moment you use it.

#Redis #WebDevelopment #FinalYearProject #BackendDevelopment #Caching #StudentDeveloper #Programming

DAY-16 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about gRPC and built a simple todo list app using it.

gRPC is a high performance RPC framework that runs over HTTP 2 and uses Protocol Buffers for defining services and message structure.

Unlike traditional REST APIs, gRPC allows streaming, which means the server can continuously send data to the client over a single connection.

In my todo app, I implemented server side streaming to read todos as a stream instead of fetching everything in a single response.

This helped me understand how streaming reduces overhead and enables more real time communication patterns in backend systems.

#BackendEngineering #gRPC #TodoApp #StreamingData #HTTP2 #ProtocolBuffers #RealTimeCommunication #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #LevelUpYourSkills

DAY-16 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about HTTP 3 and how it improves modern web communication.

Unlike HTTP 1.1 and HTTP 2 which run on top of TCP, HTTP 3 runs on top of QUIC, which is built over UDP.

By using QUIC, HTTP 3 reduces connection setup time, improves performance in high latency networks, and solves the head of line blocking problem at the transport layer.

It also integrates TLS encryption by default and supports faster handshakes, including zero round trip in some cases.

Seeing the evolution from HTTP 1.1 to HTTP 2 to HTTP 3 makes it clear how much effort goes into reducing latency and improving reliability at scale.

#BackendEngineering #HTTP3 #WebDevelopment #QUIC #Networking #TechLearning #SoftwareEngineering #LatencyReduction #TLS #ContinuousLearning

DAY-14 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned the difference between HTTP 1.1 and HTTP 2 and why HTTP 2 was introduced.

HTTP 1.1 is text based and processes requests sequentially over a single connection, which can lead to head of line blocking. Even with persistent connections, each request still waits for the previous one to finish.

HTTP 2 is binary instead of text based and introduces multiplexing, which allows multiple requests and responses to be in flight at the same time over a single TCP connection.

It also supports header compression and server push, reducing overhead and improving performance.

Understanding this difference makes it clear how protocol evolution directly impacts latency, throughput, and overall backend efficiency.

#BackendEngineering #HTTP1_1 #HTTP2 #WebDevelopment #TechLearning #ProtocolEvolution #SoftwareEngineering #PerformanceOptimization #Latency #Throughput

DAY-13 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I built a basic TCP connection to understand how reliable communication works in backend systems.

Unlike UDP, TCP starts with a proper connection setup using a handshake and maintains state between the client and server.

The connection guarantees ordered and reliable data delivery, handling retransmissions and flow control automatically.

Building this side by side with a UDP server made the differences very clear in terms of reliability, overhead, and use cases.

Hands on practice is really helping me understand why protocol choices matter in real backend architectures.

#BackendEngineering #TCP #UDP #Networking #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #Programming #DataCommunication #SystemDesign #HandsOnExperience

DAY-12 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I built a simple UDP server to practically understand how UDP works at the transport layer.

I used Node.js to create a UDP socket, bind it to a port, and listen for incoming messages from clients.

There is no connection setup, no handshake, the server simply receives packets and logs the sender’s address, port, and message.

Building this made it very clear how lightweight and stateless UDP really is compared to TCP.

Small hands on experiments like this help solidify networking concepts beyond just theory.

#BackendEngineering #NodeJS #UDP #TransportLayer #Networking #SoftwareDevelopment #HandsOnLearning #TechSkills #Programming #ContinuousLearning

DAY-11 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about the UDP protocol and its tradeoffs.

UDP is a simple, connectionless transport layer protocol. It has no handshake, is stateless, and sends data without guaranteeing delivery or order.

Because of this, it offers low latency and minimal overhead, which is why it is commonly used in online games, live streaming, DNS, and real time communication.

The downside is that UDP has no built in reliability, no retransmissions, no congestion control, and packets can be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order.

Using UDP means the application must handle these issues itself if reliability or ordering is required.

#BackendEngineering #UDPProtocol #Networking #TechLearning #SoftwareDevelopment #RealTimeCommunication #LowLatency #DataTransmission #EngineeringGrowth #ContinuousLearning

DAY-10 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about the OSI model and how it explains the complete journey of data across a network using layers.

The model has seven layers. Physical handles raw bit transmission over cables and signals. Data Link deals with frames, MAC addresses, and local network delivery. Network is responsible for logical addressing and routing, like IP. Transport manages end to end communication, reliability, and flow control, such as TCP and UDP. Session handles connection management between systems. Presentation focuses on data formatting, encryption, and compression. Application is where protocols like HTTP, FTP, and SMTP live and interact with software.

Understanding what each layer is responsible for makes it much easier to reason about network issues and backend communication problems.

This gives a strong foundation before diving deeper into real world protocols and system design.

#BackendEngineering #OSImodel #NetworkCommunication #TechLearning #SoftwareDevelopment #EngineeringMindset #NetworkingBasics #ProtocolUnderstanding #ContinuousLearning #TechEducation

DAY-9 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I learned about network protocols and why they are the foundation of all backend communication.

A protocol is simply a set of rules that define how data is exchanged between systems so both sides can understand each other correctly.

I also went through key protocol properties like how data is formatted, whether communication is one way or two way, how systems are addressed, how data is transferred, whether the protocol maintains state, and how routing is handled across networks.

Understanding these basics makes it much clearer why different protocols exist and why backend systems choose one over another depending on the use case.

#BackendEngineering #NetworkProtocols #TechLearning #SoftwareDevelopment #EngineeringFundamentals #DataCommunication #ProtocolDesign #ContinuousLearning #TechEducation #LevelUpYourSkills

DAY 8 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I dove into the Publish Subscribe or Pub/Sub model. This is a massive shift from the point to point communication patterns I have been studying so far. It introduces a message broker into the mix which decouples the sender from the receiver.

I put this into practice by setting up RabbitMQ. I built a publisher that sends jobs to a queue and a consumer that listens for those jobs to process them. It was interesting to see the asynchronous nature of this setup. The publisher does not care if the consumer is online or how long it takes to finish the job it just drops the message and moves on.

Key takeaways from today:

The publisher and consumer do not need to know anything about each other. This makes the system much more flexible and easier to scale.

If the consumer is busy or goes offline the message broker holds the jobs in a queue until the consumer is ready again.

In my specific practical I noticed that while one consumer is processing jobs any other consumer that connects has to wait if they are competing for the same queue. This is a common way to handle load where you can add more consumers to share the work but only one gets to work on a specific message at a time.

This pattern is the backbone of distributed systems and microservices where different parts of an application need to talk without being tightly coupled.

#BackendEngineering #PubSubModel #RabbitMQ #MessageBroker #AsynchronousProcessing #DistributedSystems #Microservices #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #EngineeringGrowth

DAY 7 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I explored Server Sent Events also known as SSE. This is a very interesting middle ground between the traditional request response model and full duplex WebSockets.

In an SSE setup the client establishes a long term connection with the server using a simple HTTP request. Once this connection is open the server can stream data to the client whenever it wants. Unlike WebSockets which allow two way communication SSE is unidirectional the data only flows from the server to the client.

Key takeaways from today:

Since it uses standard HTTP it works through most firewalls and proxies without any special configuration. If the connection drops the browser will automatically try to reconnect for you which is a huge plus for reliability. It is incredibly lightweight because it does not have the protocol overhead that WebSockets do.

It only allows data to flow from the server to the client. If the client needs to talk back it has to send a separate HTTP request. Most browsers have a limit on the number of open SSE connections you can have at once which can be a bottleneck for certain apps.

I find it fascinating how SSE is the perfect choice for things like live news feeds, stock tickers, or social media notifications where the user just needs to receive updates without necessarily sending data back in the same pipe.

#BackendEngineering #ServerSentEvents #SSE #WebDevelopment #RealTimeData #HTTPStreaming #TechLearning #SoftwareEngineering #WebSockets #LiveUpdates

DAY 6 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I moved from Short Polling to Long Polling to see how we can make the request-response cycle more efficient for real-time updates.

In Short Polling, the client keeps asking and the server often says nothing is new. Long Polling changes this. The client sends a request and the server hangs onto that request. It does not respond until it actually has new information or a timeout occurs. As soon as the client gets a response, it immediately sends another request to start the process over.

I modified my job status practical to see the difference. Instead of the server immediately returning the current progress, I implemented logic where the server holds the request in a pending state. Only when the background job is fulfilled does the server finally send the response back to the client.

Key takeaways from today:

It is much more efficient than short polling because it eliminates the constant noise of empty responses. 

The server only talks when it has something to say.

It feels much closer to real-time because the data is sent to the client the moment it is ready.

The server has to hold onto connections, which can be tricky to manage at high volume. 

It still follows the request-response flow, so there is still some overhead compared to a pure stream.

This was a great bridge to understand how we evolved from simple requests to more persistent communication.

#BackendEngineering #LongPolling #ShortPolling #RealTimeUpdates #EfficientCommunication #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #ProgrammingJourney #JobStatusUpdates #EngineeringBestPractices

DAY 5 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I explored Short Polling. While we usually think of the Request-Response model as a one-off interaction, Short Polling turns it into a repetitive loop to simulate real-time updates.

In this model, the client automatically sends a request to the server at fixed intervals, such as every 2 or 5 seconds, to check if there is any new data or a status update. The server responds immediately, even if nothing has changed.

I put this into practice by building a job status system. I created a submission route that adds a job to a dictionary and a status route that the client polls. To simulate a long-running process, I made the job progress by 10% every few seconds. The client keeps asking for the status until the job hits 100%.

Key takeaways from today:

Very easy to implement and works over standard HTTP without needing persistent connections like WebSockets. Good for non-critical updates where a small delay is acceptable.

It creates a lot of empty traffic. If the data hasn't changed, the server still has to process the request and send a response, which wastes resources. It is not truly real-time. The client only knows about a change after the next poll happens.

This practical helped me see exactly why this can be a bottleneck at scale and why patterns like Long Polling were created to solve the "empty response" problem.

#BackendEngineering #ShortPolling #RealTimeUpdates #RequestResponseCycle #JobStatusSystem  #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #EngineeringBestPractices #CodingJourney

DAY 4 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I took the theory of the Push model and put it into practice by building a real time chat application using plain #Nodejs and #WebSockets.

Instead of using high level libraries, I wanted to see how the connection management works at a lower level. I implemented this by maintaining an array of active connections on the server side. Every time a new browser tab opened, it acted as a unique client.

Key mechanics of the implementation:

When a new client connects, the server pushes a notification to every other active connection in the array to let them know someone new joined.

The server keeps a persistent list of all connected sockets. This is the heart of the Push model because it gives the server a direct line to every user.

When one client sends a message, the server iterates through the array and pushes that message to every other connected socket instantly.

Building this really highlighted the trade offs. While the real time speed is incredible, you can see how the backend has to work harder to keep track of every single open connection. If the array grows too large or connections drop unexpectedly, the management logic becomes much more critical.

#BackendEngineering #Nodejs #WebSockets #RealTimeChat #PushModel #ConnectionManagement #SoftwareDevelopment #CodingJourney #TechLearning #WebDevelopment

DAY 3 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I looked into the Push communication model. This is a shift from the traditional way we think about the web where a client always has to ask for data first.

In the Push model, once a connection is established, the server can send data to the client whenever new information is available. The server takes the initiative. This is how we get real-time experiences like live sports scores, stock price updates, or instant messages.

Key takeaways from today:

Real-time delivery:

 Data reaches the client almost the instant it is available on the server. 

Lower latency:

 Since the client doesn't have to keep asking for updates, there is no delay between an event happening and the client being notified. Reduced bandwidth. It can be more efficient than polling because data is only sent when it actually exists.

Resource heavy:

 The server must maintain an open connection for every single client, which can strain memory and CPU as you scale to thousands of users. Connection stability:

 If a client has a poor internet connection and the link drops, the server needs a way to handle that reconnection and potential data loss. Complexity. Implementing a robust push system requires more complex backend logic compared to a simple request-response setup.

#BackendEngineering #PushCommunication #WebSockets #RealTimeData #SoftwareDevelopment #TechLearning #ChatApplication #UserExperience #ServerClientModel #ContinuousLearning

DAY 2 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I looked into the difference between synchronous and asynchronous workloads. Understanding when to use which is one of the most important decisions in backend design because it directly impacts how a user perceives the speed of an application.

In a synchronous workload, tasks are performed one after another. The system starts a task and waits for it to finish before moving to the next one. It is straightforward and easy to debug, but if one task takes a long time, the whole process gets stuck. This is usually what happens when you wait for a page to load after clicking a button.

In an asynchronous workload, the system starts a task and immediately moves on to something else without waiting for the first task to finish. The completion of that task happens in the background. This is essential for long-running jobs like sending a heavy email, processing an image, or generating a large PDF report.

Main takeaways from today:

Synchronous is great for simple operations where you need the result immediately to proceed.

DAY 1 of levelling up my Backend Engineering Knowledge

Today I spent time breaking down the Request-Response model. While it seems simple on the surface, there is a lot happening under the hood when a client and server talk to each other.

In this pattern, the client initiates a connection and sends a formal request. The server processes that request and sends back a response along with a status code. The most important thing to remember is that the client is usually in a waiting state until that data comes back.

Key takeaways from today:

The client always starts the conversation. The server cannot send data to the client unprompted in this specific model.

It is stateless by nature. In its purest form, each request is independent and doesn't know what happened in the previous one.

It is ideal for many web applications but can be inefficient if the client needs real-time updates without constantly asking for them.

Understanding this flow is helping me see why we sometimes need to move toward other patterns like Pub/Sub or WebSockets when the waiting time becomes a bottleneck.

Day 21 – Learning Auto Scaling Groups (ASG)

What I learned:

ASG automatically adds or removes EC2 instances based on demand.

It helps maintain high availability by replacing unhealthy instances automatically.

It ensures applications can handle traffic spikes by scaling out and save money during low traffic by scaling in.

ASGs are extremely cost-effective because you only run the required number of instances at any given time, instead of keeping unnecessary servers running 24/7.

Difference between Load Balancer and ASG:

A Load Balancer (ELB) distributes incoming traffic across multiple instances.

An Auto Scaling Group (ASG) manages the number of instances ,  launching more when needed and terminating them when demand decreases.

Load Balancer = distribute traffic

ASG = add/remove instances automatically

Both work best when combined, ensuring traffic is balanced while the right number of instances is always running.

Day 19 of My Cloud Computing Journey – Exploring Types of Load Balancers

Today I dove deeper into AWS Load Balancing and learned about the different types of load balancers and their use cases. Understanding these is crucial for designing scalable and highly available applications.

 • Application Load Balancer (ALB) – operates at the application layer (Layer 7). It can route traffic based on URL paths, hostnames, or HTTP headers, making it ideal for web applications and microservices.

 • Network Load Balancer (NLB) – operates at the transport layer (Layer 4). It handles high-performance, low-latency traffic and can manage millions of requests per second, making it perfect for TCP/UDP workloads. Perfect for Gaming and Financial applications.

 • Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) – designed for third-party virtual appliances and simplifies deployment of network services like firewalls or intrusion detection systems.

Day 13 of My Cloud Computing Journey – EBS Encryption and Lifecycle Management

Today’s learning was all about EBS data protection and lifecycle management , a critical part of keeping cloud storage both secure and reliable.

I started by exploring EBS Encryption, which ensures that all data stored in a volume is automatically encrypted using AWS Key Management Service (KMS). This means everything , data at rest, data in transit between the instance and the volume, and even snapshots , stays fully protected. What’s great is that this encryption happens transparently without affecting performance or requiring manual setup.

Next, I learned about the lifecycle of an EBS volume and snapshot , when to create backups, how often to take them, and how to manage old ones efficiently. AWS recommends taking regular snapshots based on your data change frequency and business needs, whether that’s daily, weekly, or monthly.

I also explored what happens if a snapshot gets deleted accidentally. Normally, once deleted, it’s gone permanently , but AWS provides a solution for that too through the EBS Recycle Bin. By enabling a recycle bin for snapshots, you can automatically retain deleted snapshots for a specified period before they’re permanently removed. This feature can save you from major data loss caused by accidental deletions.

Today’s session made me realize that managing data isn’t just about creating and using volumes , it’s also about securing, maintaining, and protecting them over time. EBS encryption and lifecycle management are essential for building a resilient and secure cloud storage strategy.

Day 3 of My Cloud Computing Journey ||  Understanding Cloud Deployment Models

Today I learned about Cloud Deployment Models, which define how the cloud infrastructure is set up and who can access it.

There are mainly three types , and here’s how I understood them with a simple bus example:

==>Public Cloud

 Imagine a public bus , anyone can buy a ticket and use it.

 In the same way, a public cloud is shared by multiple users or organizations.

 It’s managed by cloud providers like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure, and you only pay for what you use.

 Example: Gmail, Google Drive, AWS EC2 (public access and shared infrastructure).

==>Private Cloud

 Now think of a private company bus , only employees can use it.

 Similarly, a private cloud is dedicated to a single organization.

 It offers more control and security since the resources aren’t shared with others.

 Example: An enterprise hosting its own cloud on-premises using VMware or OpenStack.

==>Hybrid Cloud

 This one is like using both public and private buses depending on the need.

 A hybrid cloud combines both public and private environments, allowing data and applications to move between them as required.

 It provides flexibility , sensitive data stays private, while other workloads can use the public cloud for scalability.

 Example: A company using AWS for hosting its website but keeping customer records in a private on-premises server.

In short:

Public Cloud → Shared and scalable

Private Cloud → Secure and controlled

Hybrid Cloud → Best of both worlds

Day 1 of My Cloud Computing Journey ,Understanding Virtualization

Today I started my cloud computing journey by exploring the core concept that makes cloud possible ,"Virtualization".

Here’s what I learned in simple terms:

Virtualization means creating multiple virtual environments or machines on a single physical system. It allows one physical computer to act like many, each running its own operating system and applications independently.

The system on which virtualization runs is called the Host Operating System, and each virtual machine created on top of it is called a Guest OS.

At the center of it all is something called a Hypervisor , a software layer that manages and allocates resources between the host and the virtual machines.

There are two main types of hypervisors:

Type 1 (Bare Metal): Installed directly on the physical hardware. These are faster and used in data centers (like VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V).

Type 2 (Hosted): Runs on top of an existing operating system. Great for local testing (like VirtualBox or VMware Workstation).

Finally, I got a clearer picture of how this idea of virtualization evolved into what we now call Cloud Computing , where instead of creating virtual machines on our own computers, we rent computing power from cloud providers like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure.

It was a solid start. Excited to continue sharing what I learn every day as I move forward in this journey.

 “Why am I not getting a job despite learning so many things?”

After going through countless rejections, failed interviews, and frustrating silences from recruiters, I realized the problem wasn’t always “the market,” “AI taking jobs,” or “too much competition.”

It was me.

 It was the things in my control that I was ignoring.

From my personal experience, here are 7 reasons most candidates struggle to land a job (and yes, I’ve been guilty of them all at some point):

==> Weak Communication Skills ,It’s not about English fluency, it’s about confidently expressing your thoughts whether in interviews, LinkedIn comments, or even a short message. Writing just “Interested” under a job post is not communication.

==> Weak Fundamentals in CS Basics . Without a solid understanding of operating systems, databases, networking, and DSA, confidence in interviews doesn’t come naturally. I learned this the hard way.

==> Jumping Between Languages , I wasted time learning Python, then Java, then JavaScript… until I realized mastery comes from holding on to one language and building real projects with it.

==> Poor Problem-Solving Skills , Computer Science = Problem Solving. If you cannot break problems into smaller chunks, coding interviews become nightmares. Strengthening my math and DSA practice made a huge difference.

==> Lack of Hands-On Projects  Watching tutorials felt productive, but I wasn’t building anything of my own. Once I started creating real, self-initiated projects, my learning accelerated , and so did recruiter interest.

==> No Real Experience  ,  “But I don’t have a job yet.” That was my excuse too. Until I explored internships, freelancing, and contributing to open source. That’s when I built credibility.

==> Generic Resume & Weak Profile , Copy-pasting resume templates got me nowhere. When I started showcasing my real work (projects, contributions, unique ideas), things changed.

 And here’s the bonus tip that completely transformed my career:

 Show Your Work Publicly.

 Share your projects, learning journey, and insights on platforms like LinkedIn, GitHub, or Twitter. That’s how recruiters started reaching out to me directly.

 At the end of the day, job hunting is like optimizing code.

 Just like we debug and optimize programs for better performance, we must also optimize ourselves fixing what’s in our control, and improving step by step.

At office a very interesting thing happened today,I thought I must share it with my fellows. A major code was pushed in the repo and the instructions I got were, pull the latest code from  develop branch (as in industry there are total 3 brances 1:Main(in production), 2:Develop (Develop & Testing)  and 3:Working(In which everyone codes and pushes)  and then run clean install, the dependencies, 

I never heard about clean install , but from my past experience , and hearing word dependencies , I knew it have something to do with npm, I asked Lead , 

should I run npm i ??  

he replied : npm ci,

i asked what is it ? and then he told me this...

npm install is a must-know tool!  

But do you really understand its twin?  

Let's break down the difference between npm install (npm i) and npm ci. 

1. npm install (npm i)  

  - Installs all dependencies listed in package.json.  

  - Updates package-lock.json if needed.  

  - Good for regular development.  

2. npm ci  

  - Uses package-lock.json for a clean install.  

  - Deletes the node_modules folder first.  

  - Perfect for CI/CD pipelines.  

Why choose one over the other?  

- Use npm install for regular updates and local development.  

- Use npm ci for consistent and clean installs in deployments.  

Understanding these commands can save you time and headaches.  

It was a new learning and new experience and the way he explained me was very facinating to me.

Django is a developer's best friend.

Django is built on key principles that reshape how we code. Here’s why it matters:

- Rapid Development: Django allows for quick iterations. You can build prototypes swiftly and refine them easily.

- Scalability: Start small, grow big. Django handles both small projects and large ones without hassle.

Django: The Python Powerhouse

- Dynamic User Interfaces: React shines when it comes to building interactive UIs. Users love the fast and responsive experiences it provides.

- Community Support: The MERN stack has a large community. This means plenty of libraries, tools, and resources are available to help you troubleshoot and innovate.

- Real-Time Data: If your project requires real-time data, MERN is often the go-to stack because of its non-blocking architecture.

Final Thoughts

If you prefer Python and need a secure backend with fast development, go for Django. If you want a full JavaScript environment and need dynamic interfaces, MERN is a solid choice.

Built a Cool App. Deployed It. Accidentally Invented a Time Machine.

Yesterday, I deployed a seemingly simple project.

 A user could add tasks, assign a date, and later filter those tasks by date.

 ==> On localhost: flawless.

 ==> On production: a mystery bug appeared.

A user reported that when they added a task at 8:00 PM, it was showing up in the database as 3:00 PM ,  a 5-hour time gap.

 Other users confirmed the same issue. I immediately opened VS Code, checked everything again , locally, it was still working perfectly.

So what went wrong?

I turned to the best senior developer we all secretly have  #ChatGPT , and started digging. Here's what I learned:

==> I was sending dates in ISO format

==> But the database (hosted on a server in a different timezone) was storing them as UTC

That was the gap. ISO + timezone difference = misaligned timestamps.

To fix it:

 ==> I converted the ISO datetime to UTC on the frontend before sending it to the database

And boom , issue resolved. The task now shows the correct time, no matter where it's saved or viewed.

Takeaway

==> Deployment isn't a destination , it's exposure to the real environment

==> Local testing doesn't account for timezone, latency, infrastructure, or edge cases

 ==> Production feedback is priceless — let real users interact with your work

Ships are meant to sail, not to rest at the docks.

 So ship your product , bugs and all , because the ocean will teach you more than the shore ever could.

Screw can be opened by a Hammer as well but we still open it with screw driver,

as knowing the right tool save us time , make the task easy and efficient.

As sir Mohammad Nauman once said in his videos:

“If you have a hammer and a screwdriver, knowing which tool to use where is the real trick.”

Sure, you can open a screw with a hammer — force it, break it, maybe even get the job done.

 But if you want it done efficiently, safely, and without future problems, you reach for a screwdriver.

I thought I had it all figured out. I realized it when I had to a task which was automatically send the reminders after some specific time.

Just a simple background task.

 Run every 5 minutes.

 Send the reminders.

 What could go wrong?

I reached for setInterval. It was fast, easy, clean.

 Minutes later, the feature was live. And it worked perfectly... for a while.

But then came the fire.

Random crashes.

 Duplicate entries.

 Unpredictable behaviors.

 Logs that made no sense.

The worst part? It only happened sometimes.

 Only in production.

 Only when I wasn’t watching.

That’s when I realized something painful:

==> setInterval doesn’t care if your app crashes. It doesn’t persist. It doesn't retry.

 ==> It runs in-memory, and once the server dies or restarts — it's gone.

 ==> Multiple intervals can accidentally stack up if you're not careful.

What I really needed was a cron job.

==> Cron jobs are built for reliability.

 ==> They run based on real time (not app uptime).

 ==> They survive restarts.

 ==> They don’t overlap unless you tell them to.

 ==> And they scale cleanly as your app grows.

I replaced the setInterval with a simple node-cron expression:

 0 */5 * * * * — every 5 minutes.

And just like that, the chaos stopped.

 No more race conditions.

 No more ghost processes.

 No more guesswork.

Lesson learned:

 Choose the right tool not just for now, but for what happens when you’re not looking.

If you’ve ever been burned by a background task…

 or spent hours debugging something that should have been simple…

 I know you’ll feel this one.

Let’s just say:

 I now respect time — both human and system time — a lot more than I used to.

Yesterday, I had a random conversation with someone on my way home...

 (If you're reading this, I hope you're not following me on LinkedIn 😅)

 Anyway, we started talking about "How do search engines return results so fast?

Most people think Google is searching the entire internet live — but that’s not really how it works. It’s actually a brilliant mix of indexing, distributed computing, and clever algorithms.

As a web developer, I find it astonishing that even though search engines seem to search the internet in real-time, they’re actually not.

Instead of crawling the web on the spot, they’re searching through massive, pre-built indexes  essentially giant, optimized databases of the web.

Here's what happens under the hood:

-- Crawling & Indexing

 Bots (aka web crawlers) constantly browse website data including text, images , heading, etc and store relevant data in a huge index.

-- Inverted Indexes

 Search engines don’t store web pages like we see them they store data in a way that lets them instantly retrieve which pages match a specific keyword.

-- Ranking Algorithms

 When you search, complex algorithms rank pages based on relevance, freshness, backlinks, and more  all in less than a  second.

So next time you get a result in 0.3 seconds, remember: it's not magic it's brilliant engineering.

Debounce vs Throttle –– Same Same, But Different 😂 ?

It took me several tutorials and a few hours with ChatGPT to understand this concept, but you'll understand it in just 3 mins.

--Debouncing:

Debouncing means delaying the execution of a function until a certain period of inactivity — for example, until the user stops typing.

Let’s say we want to search for a product from a large JSON object. We've passed the search keyword as a dependency in the useEffect hook, so the search function gets called every time the user presses a key.

--The problem?

 The function gets executed way more times than necessary, which leads to unnecessary rerenders and performance lags, unresponsive UI errors — especially if the JSON is huge.

--The solution — Debouncing:

 We delay the function execution until the user finishes typing. So instead of running on every keystroke, the function runs only once when the user stops.

This results in:

Fewer function calls

Which ultimately results in improved performance and smoother UI.

--Throttling:

On the other hand, throttling means calling a function at regular intervals not more frequently than a defined delay (like once every 300ms), even if the event keeps firing.

Let me give you a real example:

Imagine in an e-commerce project, we have a button that places an order. When clicked, the frontend sends a POST request containing:

Product ID, color, name, user ID, name, address, phone, email, payment info, quantity, notes, etc.

Now, while the backend is busy saving this data to the database, the user might click the button multiple times. This can:

-- Send duplicate requests

 -- Overload the backend

 -- Cause unexpected behavior or even crashes (if try & catch are not used intelligently)

One way to handle this is by throttling the button click handler allowing only one request every few milliseconds.

(Though a better solution might be disabling the button after one click, throttling can still help as an extra safety net.)

Another great use case is infinite scrolling (e.g., YouTube, Instagram, Facebook). If a user scrolls too fast, the app might fire tons of requests to fetch new data.

With throttling, we can limit how often scroll-triggered functions run — reducing backend load and improving performance.

So in a nutshell use debounce when you want to reduce unnecessary calls, and throttle when you need to control the frequency of actions.

Is JavaScript Compiled or Interpreted? The Answer Might Surprise You!!!

When working with programming languages, we often categorize them as:

1:Compiled Languages (C, C++)

2:Interpreted Languages (Python)

In compiled languages, a compiler translates the entire code into machine code before execution. The compiled program runs as a whole, making it faster but requiring compilation beforehand.

On the other hand, an interpreter reads and executes code line by line at runtime, making execution flexible but often slower compared to compiled languages.

What Makes JavaScript Different?

JavaScript does not fit strictly into either category. Instead, it uses a technique called Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation.

Initially, JS interprets the code, just like an interpreter. However, it identifies frequently used parts of the code and compiles them into optimized machine code, just like a compiler. This compiled code is reused, avoiding repetitive interpretation and significantly improving execution speed.

How Does This Work?

Let's take an example:

Imagine a function that adds two numbers. When calling the function, we pass two numbers to be added.

Without JIT Compilation:

The JavaScript engine interprets the function every time it is executed.

With JIT Compilation:

The engine detects that the add function is used multiple times in the code. It compiles it into optimized machine code and reuses it for faster execution.

Why Does This Matter?

Various JavaScript engines, like V8 (Chrome, Node.js, MS Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), and JavaScriptCore (Safari), use JIT Compilation to make JavaScript execution faster and more efficient.

This is what makes JavaScript unique—combining the best of both worlds (interpreted and compiled) to deliver better performance and speed.

How Web Workers Can Speed Up Your Website and Enhance User Experience?

Have you ever had a webpage freeze while :

-loading large datasets

-running complex calculations

-processing images? 

That lag happens because JavaScript is single threaded language ,which means  that  it handles everything i.e: UI updates, rendering, and logic on a single thread. When heavy tasks run on this same thread, the browser can become unresponsive.

To solve this, Web Workers were introduced in HTML5. They allow JavaScript to execute tasks in the background on a separate thread, preventing UI lag. Instead of slowing down your app, these tasks run independently, keeping the interface smooth and responsive.

How Do Web Workers Work?

Web Workers are basically background assistants, they take care of high computations while your main thread on which the UI or Javascript is being executed,  stays focused on user interactions. For example, if your app needs to parse a large JSON file or perform realtime data processing, a Web Worker can handle it without freezing the UI.

When Should You Use Web Workers?

1:Complex mathematical Formulas eg: finding largest prime number.

2:Reading/Writing large data from localstorage/Database

3:Processing Images/Videos etc.
